reading.body:
One lobbyist's AI filings reach 31 clients, and the largest single share of them is semiconductor and hardware companies, not the software firms the AI debate usually names.

The client list is broad but not random. It runs from chipmakers (Advanced Micro Devices, Texas Instruments, IBM) through cloud and security (Cloudflare, Palo Alto Networks, Rapid7) to trade groups (ITI, the Retail Industry Leaders Association, the Business Roundtable) and to sectors that would be regulated by AI rules rather than build them: Medtronic, Mayo Clinic, New York-Presbyterian, the National Fair Housing Alliance, Procter & Gamble. The counts are small per client, mostly five to nine filings, which is consistent with a portfolio practice rather than a single-issue campaign.

For AI specifically, the pattern matters because it shows where the money for influence sits relative to the compute stack. Chips, cloud, and enterprise software are all represented here. The one power-adjacent name is the Edison Electric Institute, on five filings, which is the only entry in this data that touches the electricity side of the buildout. Nothing in the record shows what was lobbied for, only who was represented and how often.

What this does not tell you: the subject matter of any filing, the bills or agencies involved, the amounts spent, or the outcome. It also does not establish that these clients coordinate. The prior government position is disclosed as required by the Lobbying Disclosure Act, and the data records it without indicating when it was held or how it relates to the filings.
